utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I do understand that there are some bar table movements continuing at this moment, and I do understand that Mr. Registrar will provide us soon with a complete list in a memo so that we can further deal with the matter after the Chamber has looked at the documents as well. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one more that I have not alerted the registrar to, I don't believe. We have sent it to the Prosecution. It is a compilation that we did in response to a question posed by Judge Kinis. If I may call it up and tender it, it is 1D38-0004. This is a document, it's a compilation from a document that's well over a thousand pages long so we put together a compilation. It is related to the 18 or -- it's meant to address the 18 August 1995 order of Mr. Moric which was the subject of a question by Judge Kinis several days ago. It is criminal complaints that were filed by the MUP after the 18th of August for crimes that were committed before the 18th of August. And it is from the various police administrations and police stations that were subject of the Moric order of the 18th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said criminal complaints. The list however says list of charges filed against. From my understanding a charge filed is not exactly the same as a criminal complaint lodged. And from what I remember is that for some of them it says decision by the state prosecutor's office conviction. I wasn't aware that prosecutors also are convicting, but I'm just trying to understand what we have been presented with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will actually check that, Your Honour, but I think it -- let me clarify that category, Your Honour. I -- but it is meant obviously category 8 is what we're talking about in terms of how the proceedings ultimately wound up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ended, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it is more or less -- it has been extracted from the long list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. We tender it, Your Honour. I'm going to be contacting Mr. Margetts, because Mr. Tieger and I had a conversation. I'm not sure -- they have some documents from the state attorney's offices but if they need the underlying document we will be happy to give it to the Prosecution so they can review it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that is correct, Your Honour. As Mr. Misetic indicated we will I think require the underlying document and will be looking at that and will need some opportunity to both review this document and the underlying materials before we can respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And how much dime do you think you would need for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In fairness, Your Honour, I -- given the size of the underlying materials, perhaps it would be more prudent to take a quick look and get back to the Court before suggesting arbitrarily a particular time. I think I'm likely to overestimate the amount of time out of caution without seeing the materials but once we see them I think we can give a more realistic assessment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that could be two, three day so you can give a realistic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- assessment of the time you would need. Okay. Then that's on the record. I take that we need a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes exhibit number D568.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D568 is then marked for identification for the time being, Mr. Registrar. Then any other procedural matter. If not, Mr. Hedaraly, are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We are, Your Honour, just before, during the re-examination of Mr. Janic last week there was a document that was shown and not tendered. That is 65 ter 1417, and the Prosecution would like to tender it at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. To be quite honest to you, it does not immediately come to my mind what 65 ter 1417 is. Could we just have a brief look at it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's -- is there any --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is the publication giving information about the functioning of Croatian institutions and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And it is it a document of what size, because we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I believe it's 45 pages and we would tender the whole document because we will be relying on various portions of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that's the document which is already in two languages because I see on my screen that it is 76 pages, but most likely half in English, half in B/C/S. Yes, it is page by page half English half B/C/S. But it is not a 45-page document, apparently. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes exhibit number P588.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P588 is admitted into evidence. Since there are no objections. Mr. Hedaraly, apart from this issue, are you ready or will it be Mr. Russo to call the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It will be me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, the witness, as I saw, prefers to express himself in French, although he gave his statement and signed his statement in English. Do you have any idea whether he prefers to speak French or English in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I believe he will testify in French, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In French. And MR. HEDARALY: And because it is the 14th of July, I will be asking questions in French as well to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course I do understand. I didn't know that it was celebrated in Canada as well. But -- Mr. Usher, can you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hello, Mr. Gilbert.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hello.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I understood you well, you would rather speak French.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you testify, our procedures -- our procedure requires us that you make a solemn declaration. The text will be handed to you by our usher. I apologise for my French. I will not continue in French. You would rather speak French, and I think I would rather speak English. But I will follow your testimony in French.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will say the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. You may sit down. Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Before Mr. Usher sits down, if I can give him a copy of his statements and exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Good morning, captain.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Could you please give us your name for this transcript?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: My name is Alain Gilbert.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Captain Gilbert, do you remember having been interviewed by the investigators of the OTP on January 29, 2008?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you made a statement to the OTP based on this interview statement which you signed on February 5, 2008?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: You re-read this statement yesterday? Have you read this statement once again yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Does this statement reflect faithfully what you told to the OTP during the interview with the investigator?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And what -- the content of this statement reflects the truth, as far as you know, as far as --

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Finally, if the same questions were put to you again today, same questions of those that were asked when you were interviewed by the OTP, would you answer in the same way?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could I have document 5319 be on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Captain Gilbert, could you confirm that the statement that we see now on the screen is the one that we mentioned earlier?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could the document 5319 be tendered into evidence under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes exhibit number 589.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P589 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we could please have 65 ter 5215, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, you have heard the request to slow down for the interpreters? No. Well, now you have. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Gilbert, we see an aerial photograph on the screen. Is this the base of the UN in Knin in 1995?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: On this picture, you circled in red the place where your office was. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If I could now have 65 ter 5335, please. Can I have the assistance of Mr. Usher to provide a photograph for the witness to place on the ELMO. There seems to be a problem with uploading in e-court, but they are going to be resolving it shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, is 65 ter 5335, is that an article written by this witness, which you sought to be uploaded, or is it something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It is a picture. A photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the one that we have now on our screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Gilbert, do we see the -- does this photograph represent the base of the UN in Knin?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes, part of it in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If I could have the assistance of the Mr. Usher so the witness can mark this picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gilbert, with the electronic pen, could you please circle your office on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can you please a B next to it for B like bureau, office in French.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Unfortunately, my French is not what it should be. We got the French translation on the English channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. I was listening to the English as well. But what Mr. Hedaraly asked is to have the two documents to be admitted under one number. That is the aerial photograph and this photograph marked by the witness where his office was marked with the letter B.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There's no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection to that. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes exhibit number P590.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P590, consisting of one aerial photograph and one photograph marked by the witness, is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to tender the following exhibits that are joined to the statement. 65 ter 5214, those are the notes made by the witness on the morning of August 4, 1995. 65 ter 5216, the text of an article written by this witness. And exhibit 438 which is the minutes of a meeting held on August 4th by General Forand and the representative of the RSK. All these documents are attached to the statement and the basis for their tendering can be find in the statement of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, one by one first --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have no objection to any of those exhibits. I would ask that they be subsequently numbered as opposed to one bulk number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's how I understood Mr. Hedaraly's request, to have them one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, first the notes, I do understand handwritten notes made by the witness on the morning of the 4th of August, 5214.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This becomes exhibit number P591, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P591 is admitted into evidence. The next one being 438, minutes of a meeting held on August the 4th with General Forand and representative of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This becomes exhibit number P592, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P592 is admitted into evidence. And then the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that was 5216.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That becomes exhibit number P593, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P593 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: For your information, there is one document that is joined and is mentioned on paragraph 28 of this statement, but it has already been tendered into evidence as D197 -- D297.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We are informed now. That's what you said, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could have 65 ter 5336 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Captain Gilbert, let me show you a few photographs that were taken from the third floor balcony of the UN base in Knin. This will soon be on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Does this photograph show part of what you saw from your office when looking at Knin?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes. This picture was taken from the balcony. If I remember well, the window of my office must have been about ten metres off on the right. But this is what I would see from my window.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: In the notes that you made on the morning of August 4th as well as in your statement, paragraph 15, for example, you refer, and I will say -- quote in English, because your notes are in English [Previous translation continues] ... building. [Interpretation] In your statement you say that you were using that parliament white building as a reference. Can you see it on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Could our usher please help us once again so that the witness can mark the document and if you could circle it red, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, could we please have a indicate that the photograph was taken? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It was last year, I believe, in the fall of 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge, my recollection is that it is in late November of 2007. I think that's about right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. That would be the fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you kindly place the letter P alongside the parliament building, please?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we save this photograph and move on to the next photograph. It's a series of three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, do you want at a later stage to tender the unmarked photograph as well or just the marked version?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: There will be two marked and one unmarked, and I will tender the series of two marked and one unmarked as one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I now have the unmarked version again on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: The second page of this document should be a different picture. Here we go. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Captain Gilbert, this photograph is a view you had from your balcony slightly to the right. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... of that document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, Captain, in this picture we see the view or part of the view you had from your office on the 4th of August, 1995. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes. I realise on looking at this photograph that there were two balconies in front of the building. My office was on the right-hand side ten metres away. So, in fact, it's a second balcony which I indicated a while ago. My office was to the right of that and that was a view I had from my window.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: In your notes and in your statement in paragraph 17 and 18, you refer to a small hill. In English you say [In English]... hill. [Interpretation] Can you tell us whether you can see this small hill you referred to?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: It's certainly one of those two hills, but on looking at this photograph I don't know which hill is the smallest. But in paragraph 17 what I mentioned was that it was behind the smallest of the two hills. Or hillocks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to tender these three photographs into evidence. And I would like just one exhibit number. The first photograph was marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge. That one question will be a little confusing on cross, so I would ask that we put separate numbers for these photos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to -- I was confused by the answer about the two balconies. First question: Are all the photographs taken from the same balcony?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes, they are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then, Mr. Gilbert, was this balcony which we see prominently in the front of this picture, was that the balcony in front of your office or is it the one in the back that was in front of your office? I see two balconies on this photograph, the one from which the photograph is taken and other one further away. Which one is the one in front of your office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The one which is the furthest away, my window did not give on to the balcony but on to the window next door. So to be very precise, it's a window which is to the right-hand side five metres approximately from the furthest -- the balcony that is the furthest away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it is the -- I don't know whether it is one building or two buildings, but at least the balcony further away was the balcony of the building your office was in, but, you say, your office did not give entrance to the balcony but was to the right of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. And that -- we're talking about the same building. It's one and the same building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Apparently two parts of that building, I can't see that on this photograph. Then I have one further question: To the right of that further away balcony seen from the building or facing the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the furthest away from what we see on this photograph at this moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, we have now three photographs. The first one marked by the witness, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar suggests, and I'm inclined to follow him, that we first have the unmarked photograph with just a tiny little bit of the corner of the balcony and that would be, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's 65 ter 05336 and becomes exhibit number P594.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P594 is admitted into evidence. Now the second exhibit is the same photograph but now marked by the witness with the white parliament building.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That becomes exhibit number P595, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's not the one that's on our screen at the moment but P594 -- no, I'm -- the second exhibit now, the photograph marked by the witness is P595 and is admitted into evidence. The next one, unmarked photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes exhibit number P596.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P596 is admitted into evidence. And, finally, the last one with the two balconies.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That becomes exhibit number P597, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P597 which we now see on our screen is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Could we go back to P590. Captain, I'd like to clarify what you have just said to the Presiding Judge of this Chamber. The balcony from which the photographs were taken, the balcony we've just seen, are those the balconies that we see on the right hand of this building here?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes. I can tell you where it is if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: To the right-hand side of this building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to read a short summary of the witness's statement, and I shall read it out in English. [In English] Alain Gilbert was an officer in the Canadian armed forces stationed in Knin in 1995 with UNCRO as General Alain Forand's aide-de-camp. On the morning of 4 August 1995, he observed the shelling of Knin from his office on the top floor of the UN headquarters. He recorded some of his observations regarding the shelling that morning in his notebook, including the fact that MRLs were used at 5.00 a.m. In addition, he also provides evidence on the shelling on the morning of the 5th of August, 1995, and, in particular, an initial barrage of approximately 400 shells that fell between 5.19 and 5.25. Mr. Gilbert also noticed burning and looting in Knin and around after Operation Storm. He became the refugee officer at the UN camp on 25 August 1995, and his impression was that most of the Serbs wanted to go back to their houses but were afraid of doing so for their safety. This concludes my summary, Your Honours, as well as my direct examination. [Interpretation] Thank you, Captain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Hedaraly. Mr. Kehoe, I take it that you would like to have the lectern.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE

utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just get a little situated I'll be ready to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gilbert, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Kehoe, who is counsel for Mr. Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, captain. I would like to ask you a few questions from your statements and from your article and if we jump around a little bit just bear with me, but I would direct your attention to the documents before you as we go through things. Now, the first item that I would like to talk to you about, Captain, is the statement that you make in paragraph 36 of your statement, 589. Now, captain, you had come to Knin on the 8th of July and you note in your -- paragraph 36 that there were no Croats living in Knin in August of 1995. Now, when you were in Knin, did you talk to the Serb population as to why there were no Croats living in Knin?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No. This was through our briefings in the morning which we had at the UNHCR and cooperation meetings that this information was conveyed to me, I arrived in Knin rather, on the 28th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am mistaken if I read in paragraph 36 that five per cent of -- oh, no. I see that, now I see that. It's the last line, yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, I mean, did you converse with the Serb population in Knin prior to Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Not really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you say "not really," what do you mean, not really? Did you talk to them?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No. The only people were employees in the camp that were Serb, but I didn't speak to any locals, any local Serbs living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when you -- when you spoke to the Serbs that were in the camp did you ask them what happened to the Croats in Knin?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No. But I know -- I did know what happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What did you know?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Undoubtedly, more than undoubtedly, they were expelled from the town of Knin in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now let me focus in on the time-frame prior to Operation Storm and, if I may, I'd like to direct your attention to your article which is P593.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we could bring that up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is a -- page 3 in the English. I'm not sure what it is in the French.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It's tab 5 in the binder the witness has, just for --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, counsellor. I don't know how Your Honour wants to handle this between the B/C/S and the English and the French, but I just ask for Your Honours's guidance as to what comes up on the screen. I'm going to obviously deal with the English version and the witness can deal with either one, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And if there would be any -- if they're not fully congruent, then we will --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I'm dealing, captain, with the third page in the English about middle of the way down and you're talking about the shelling on the 1st of August and note about -- about the individuals coming to the camp. Women, children, and old people who had not left the night before, either by personal choice or because they had no means of transport, were hiding in the basement. And I wanted to talk to about your comment there, had not left the night before. And I take it that, sir, you know then Major Bellerose, do you not?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: It's a major, yes, he is a major. Not --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the Article is the 4th of August, not the 1st of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My apologies. I was talking about the 4th. If I said the 1st, I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Major Bellerose in his diary, and this is exhibit 513, noted on the 28th of July of 1995 that the locals were leaving the area. I'm going to go through a sequence of events, captain, and just ask you some questions about it. Again, on the 29th of July, again in D513, Major Bellerose said that the people in Knin are very nervous, a lot of them are leaving town and refugees from Bosansko Grahovo are arriving.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think we had last week once again, that if the testimony or something of someone else is being shown to confront the witness, the question should be asked of him. He talked about the 4th in his article. I think he should first be asked if he has any knowledge of these people on the 29th of July and then be confronted with Mr. Bellerose's statement or diary or testimony. I think that's what we had this discussion last week about and Your Honour referred to a transcript portion of a few weeks ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we did not have the discussion in this fashion and what I'm doing is highlighting a sequence of events of items that have come into evidence with Prosecution witnesses and then asking the witness based on what he said in his article. Now, this is not the sequence of events as presented by the Prosecution. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: But he has not testified or brought any evidence on the 28th of July, so he should first be asked the question given a chance to then be confronted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly is asking you to first, without referring to other evidence, to elicit from the witness what he knows about the event, and only after that, to put to him what other evidence --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is items that are already in evidence and are part of the record. What I am doing is bringing to this witness's attention items that are part of the record and then asking him questions based on evidence in the record. That's what I'm doing here in an expeditious form, as opposed to taking these items sequentially. The jumping off point is his comment that these people had left the night before and I am simply taking him through a sequence of events or items that have come into evidence already. This is not something that I'm pulling out that hasn't come in from a Prosecution witness already.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That apparently is not the issue. The issue apparently is that Mr. Hedaraly, and I would have to review exactly what we said about that, if you could give me a source, Mr. Hedaraly, I'll try to find it. The issue is that prior to putting to the witness what is in evidence already, first ask the witness without putting that to him what he knows about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will take the long way around and this is going the long way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, I wasn't finished speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I asked --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Hedaraly to give me the reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I was responding to a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So at that moment, I think, Mr. Hedaraly, polite approach would have been not to interrupt Mr. Kehoe. At the same time I thank you for finding the point -- the reference for me. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe. And I'll check exactly what was said for this first question, if you take what you call the long route.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Captain Gilbert, on the 28th of July, did you see a general mobilisation of ARSK soldiers in Knin?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So when a Prosecution witness Major Bellerose wrote in his diary on 28th July general mobilisation is happening in town, you don't know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean. These are the words spoken by Major Bellerose. I don't remember that there was such a general mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I'm sorry for interrupting you, but due to the quick exchange of views now the reference doesn't appear on the transcript, so I have difficulties in finding it. Could you please, Mr. Hedaraly, repeat the reference you just gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I will do in a second, Your Honour. I'm just getting a little lost myself. If you'll just give me a few minutes I'll be able to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine, but please not by interrupting Mr. Kehoe. Wait until he has finished his sentences. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Captain, were you aware that on the 28th of July that Bosansko Grahovo had fallen to the HV?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No. I don't remember the operational sequence of the various parties present. This was not part of my job. I don't remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you aware, Captain that on the 28th of July, the president of the Republic of Serb Krajina, Milan Martic, declared a state of war throughout the entire Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I don't remember anything of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Staying on the 28th, were you aware that the local population was leaving the area?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: It's quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you, did you know it or did you not?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hedaraly. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, again going further, on the 29th of July, moving yet closer to Operation Storm, were you aware in Knin that the civilian population was leaving?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: It's likely that the population in Knin was beginning to leave around those dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, tell us what you know about that, captain, about the population leaving Knin around those dates.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Well, there was a state of panic of a sort in Knin. There were rumours circulating and saying that there would be a Croatian attack against Knin in the next few weeks or days. In fact, together with General Forand, when we did our rounds and visits the UN forces, we were called back to the camp, because there was some emergency. There was something going on, because there was a state of panic in Knin. I could say that there was a -- a likely attack on the part of the Croatian on the 28th and 29th of July. I believe that the civilian population had started to leave Knin already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And did they leave -- and how did the civilian population leave?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Whichever way they could, and they crossed through Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Captain, did this exodus of the civilian population continue from the 28th and the 29th through the eve of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you would agree, sir, that the exodus of the civilian population throughout Knin all this time was quite extensive, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I don't agree with you particularly, but there was an exodus of the people living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, during this same time-frame did you also see a build-up of military personnel and military vehicles in and around the Knin area?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... read you the testimony of another Prosecution witness, Jan Elleby, who was a CIVPOL police officer who noted that now as we move -- this is on page 3474. "Question: Now as we move through July of 1995 you note in your supplemental information sheet, and it says well, actually -- I think it begins on P214, that you saw a lot of soldiers on the street but in your supplemental sheet you observed an increased number of RSK troops in Knin in this period. In the period building up to Operation Storm, can you tell us about that a little?" "Answer: Yes. The assessment of the picture in the streets in the town was that from a few days in July up to the end of July, that there came more and more military vehicles, more and more uniformed military personnel." "Question: And did you and other CIVPOL monitors observe that while you were driving around the area?" "Answer: Yes." Is that informing by Mr. Elleby consistent with your observations in Knin at the latter part of July?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: That information stems from Mr. Elleby. That's what he remembers from those times. I don't remember a huge build-up as this gentleman has mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, there was a military presence in Knin, wasn't there, prior to Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes, there was a military presence. There was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm sorry. And that military presence, sir, was quite significant, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No. I can't quantify it any way and say it was significant or not. I know that there was a military presence since one could come across soldiers when one went to the residence, from the camp to the residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, as of the 5th of August the speculation in UN Sector South was that Knin would not fall until 48 hours later and possibly not till a week later. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: What I remember is that it might have been 24 hours, 48 hours, a week before, or even more. So that is right. If you say 24, 24 hours, 48 hours, that's right. Personally, I thought that might have been a bit longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's turn directly to your article and go to page 4 in the English. The first full paragraph after the carry-over paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: [In English] The one that start with: "We expect"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, sir. I'm just waiting for it to come up on the screen, captain, if I may. The second sentence in: "At 5th August at 0519, 1995, another intensive artillery barrage, more than 500 shells fall on the town in six minutes. The forecast of when the Croatian forces will arrive in Knin proceed apace. 48-72 hours to one week or more." So the belief in Sector South was that there was at least another 48 hours before Knin was going to fall. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what people believed in Sector South, but that's what I believed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that belief was based on the fact that you thought that the ARSK had the military strength in Knin to fight off the HV for between 48 to 72 hours to one week. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes. But I believed it was a matter of defending Knin from the outside and protecting it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the -- Knin was in fact defended out on various front line areas, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I don't think that Knin was defended by several front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, there was a front line, was there not, that was manned by the RSK with both personnel and artillery. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Probably. I don't know where those lines were, but we have every reason to believe that the RSK had soldiers there that were defending that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is your testimony, Captain, that you don't know where the front lines were and where the ARSK positions were on the front line?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: When I was there, we visited some of the positions, some of the Serb positions and some of the Croatian positions with our aides and liaison officer, but I cannot describe to you the front lines and the Serb defence line as they were protecting Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, you knew that they were on the front line but you don't know where the front line was? And I'm talking about the ARSK now.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: That's correct. We don't know what the -- how many soldiers they had either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So if -- if I can just take that once step further, if there was shelling somewhere on the front line between the ARSK and the HV, you wouldn't know who was shelling whom, would you? You would just hear it?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question again. I had a problem with the translation. I would like to hear it in English, please. Could I have it again, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Absolutely, captain. And if at any time that you don't understand one of my questions, just tell me, okay? Captain, so if there was shelling going on on the front line between the HV and the ARSK and you were hearing this from the UN Sector South headquarters, you wouldn't know who was firing on whom, would you, because you didn't know where these positions on the front lines were?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I was in the Knin camp, on -- the artillery fire from the 4th and 5th of July went over our camp and reached Knin. So I knew that these shots came from the south. But I cannot believe that this would be anything other than Croatian artillery fire that was over our heads and landed in Knin, but I didn't know exactly where the front lines were but I was able to detect where the shots came from and where they landed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was there shelling going on on the front line area, Captain?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I don't know about that. Probably. But this was not part of my responsibilities. There was certainly some firing on the front lines, but I wasn't involved in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you were in the UN Sector South headquarters, could you hear it?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: On the 4th and 5th of August, yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when you heard this firing on the front line, isn't it a fact that you don't know who was firing on whom, do you?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I knew who was firing at who. The -- the shooting came from the south, went over our heads, and fell on Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, sir. Let us pull up P102. Captain, this is UN sitrep report from UNMO's headquarters Sector South dated 4th August at 2000 hours. If we can go three pages in, the bottom of the page. Reports from KenBat. You know the KenBat locations, captain?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: You're talking about KenBat or CanBat 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you today where that was. But, yes, I knew where the Kenyans were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: They were between Strmica and up on the Dinara, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I can't tell that you. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just bear with me here, Colonel. As of -- this is 2000 hours on the 4th. There are 1230 bomb reports from the Kenyan Battalion, 638 from the ARSK, 592 from the HV HVO. Do you have any idea whether or not when you were in UN Sector South if you heard that type of artillery fire taking place?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have problems with the translation. Could you tell me the question in English again, please? Could you repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sure. Let me just read it to you again. I think it might be on your screen. As of -- this is it 2000 hours on the 4th there are 1230 bomb reports from the Kenyan Battalion, 648 from the ARSK, 592 from the HV HVO. Do you have any idea whether or not you -- when you were in UN Sector South you heard that type of artillery fire taking place?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I didn't hear the firing. I certainly couldn't have heard the firing coming from the Kenyans.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is it your testimony, sir, that you could not hear artillery fire from the location of the Kenyan Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I don't know. Your Honour, as far as I remember, the Kenyan positions were far removed. I can't tell you exactly where they were compared with our headquarters in Knin. But the shots that fell and the shots that could be fired, I'm talking about artillery fire in the Kenyan sector, well, those shots, I did not hear. That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Let us turn our attention, and we'll get back that in a bit when we start talking about the artillery that you did in fact observe in Knin and we'll talk a little bit about this. And let us go to the evening of the 3rd. Do you know that on the evening of the 3rd, Colonel Leslie talked to Major Dussault and they told Mr. Bellerose, and this is it in P546. They went into the ops room and Mr. Bellerose say I went into the operations room to speak to them and they told me that they had received a message stating that something was likely to happen the following day. Now, do you recall Colonel Leslie telling General Forand that he had received that message at 2300 and that something was likely to happen the following day?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about this, about this discussion and I don't know whether Colonel Leslie said that to General Forand or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, had he told General Forand that, you being General Forand's aide-de-camp, would you have known about it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, one second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, he answered the question. Now it's calling for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I took the question as if he had told Forand, would this gentleman, this captain who was his aide-de-camp, would he have known about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, of course it is speculative to the extent that we do not know whether it was told to Mr. Forand and therefore not whether the message could have been passed to Mr. Gilbert. At the same time, Mr. Kehoe is asking if you'd look at it in a more general way as to whether information received by Mr. Forand would, under normal circumstances, read -- reach Mr. Gilbert, and that question is admissible. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Kehoe, may I take that that's what you wanted to ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you choose the right formulation right away, then Mr. Hedaraly is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, no, Your Honour I was just waiting for the usher to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. I meant if you initially had formulated the question as I did it and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yours was much better, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It avoids objections by Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you understand? Do you want me to repeat the question, captain?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, if you're allowed to do it, do it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Captain, in the normal course of events, if Colonel Leslie had called General Forand at 2300 hours on the 3rd of August and told him that he received a message that something was likely to happened the following day, is that something that you would in the normal course of events have known about?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Most probably because at that time my recollection is that we were at the residence at 2200 at that time and I would have known because I was at the residence, if it is something that they would have discussed at the headquarter earlier, maybe I would not have been informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, what time did you get the call from Sector South headquarters that something was going to happen?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I said headquarter in my deposition. I'm not 100 percent sure but it was from a headquarter so it could be Canadian, it could be Zagreb, or it could be Sector South. I think in Sector South and it was at 0330 hour on the 4th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what time was it that you left to -- with General Forand to go back to Sector South headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Around 0400.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, prior to you leaving, did General Forand give any order, you know, to warn other UN personnel that they should get back to the base?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No. No specific UN personnel other than the -- that there was one, the -- the Czech colonel living on the first floor in the same residence we were, so he left with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Captain, at this time, there were people that were staying in the UN camp, weren't there? For safety reasons, I mean.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You don't recall that?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: More than I don't recall. I don't think so. There was nobody living in our camp for safety reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In the days -- in the days leading up to Operation Storm, Captain, was there any preparations going on within Sector South headquarters to ensure that -- that there was extra food and extra water and that people had bags backed and the APCs were ready to pick up UN personnel if an attack took place? Were any of those preparations being made?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I don't know about the preparation itself. Now I find out that I speak in English, I hope it is fine. I don't think that there were any specific preparation taking place, but, as I said earlier, at one point we were called back in the camp because there would be an attack coming the next day. So we know there was a feeling that there was something that would happen. Where, not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the information you got about the attack was an hour and a half before the actual attack took place?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yeah, 0330.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let me talk to you a little bit about your testimony and about the actual shelling itself. And if we can go through this, you note in your -- in your statement at -- if I may, paragraph 9 that you not an artillery expert. And before we go into this shelling I'd just like to ask you a few things. You note in paragraph 9 that in your estimation most of the shelling came from a 155-millimetre or a 203-millimetre. Do you see, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, what type of 155, what it was?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Heavy artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No. I'm just asking was it a Howitzer or a gun. Or do you know?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I don't know if it was a Howitzer or a gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, whether or not it's a Howitzer or a gun has a lot to do with the range. Has everything to do with the range of the weapon, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And at the time that the shelling was taking place on the morning of the 4th, was Knin within range of 155?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes, I would say yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what was the range?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I would say approximately 25 kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So your testimony -- well, let me be more specific. If the HV only had a 155 Howitzer, what's the range on a 155 Howitzer?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I said I'm not sure, but I would estimate that the range is 25 kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would you surprise, sir, to learn that it's about 17 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No, I would not be surprised and I don't know if it is true, but I'm not surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. If it was within 17, a 155 would not have been within range of Knin from the positions of the HV on the morning of the 4th, would it?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I don't know where the position of the HV were on the morning of the 4th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How about the 203s. You maintain there was a 203 being used. What's the range on a 203?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I would estimate over 35 kilometre, approximately 35 kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You're testimony is that the range on a 203 is 35 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No. I said I'm not sure. So I would estimate it as 35 kilometre because you are asking me to estimate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So if there -- if in fact the -- would you be surprised to learn that the range of a 203 is less than 20 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No, I'm not surprised and I don't know if it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. So when you tell us it's 35 kilometres, you really don't know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now that they're both speaking English, the French was a little slower, so just pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're now speaking the same language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we would have take a little pause between question and answer and answer and question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. So when you said 35 kilometres, Captain, for a 203 that's pure speculation on your part, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No, that is not pure speculation. What I wrote on that paragraph with 155 and 203-millimetre artillery is more about the damage and explosion that I saw on the ground than the actual range of the gun itself. But, as I said earlier, it was coming from 15 to 35 kilometre, my estimation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And well, we can just let the record stand the way it is. But you don't really know what the range of a 203 is, do you?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: But as I said, I said I would guess or approximate it at 35 kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now let's just talk a little bit about your observations at the time. And if we can go to your notes, if I may, and I'm dealing with P591. Now, when the shelling actually started at 5.01, you were actually walking around the camp, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Are you referring to a specific paragraph or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: -- I don't know the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I may, sir, if you can go to paragraph 5 in your statement. Paragraph 5: "It was during this tour of the camp that the first shells fell on Knin."

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yeah, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. So your notations here that you have in P591 started at 5.02 were something that you wrote after the fact, right, after you had finished walking around the camp, ran back at the headquarters and went back upstairs, right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And as a matter of fact, you have no notations whatsoever in here between 5.02 and 5.38?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the fact is, sir, that when you offered an opinion as to the amount of shelling that was going on, these were your rough estimates because even from your notes we just note this gap between 5.02 and 5.38, and if I can continue on your notes stop at approximately 9.30. You can take a look at your notes, 591, I believe you can see the third page, that your actual notes stop. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So what you have given us is your rough approximation -- let me withdraw that a second. How much time did you spend up in the window or on the balcony looking at this?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I would estimate from 5.02 to noon and to come back later on the afternoon, you know, I don't have really a recollection but I spend most of the time there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But the -- you stopped talking notes at 9.30 and then you began to do other things later on in the morning with General Forand, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No, it's not correct. I don't know why the register ended at 0923. May I say that the reason why me taking those notes on that morning has nothing to do with coming here and giving an official testimony of the number of shell that landed in Knin on the 4th and the 5th of August. It is some notes that I took, and it does not reflect the exact amount of shell that were fired on Knin on the 4th and the 5th, but it is the note that I took on that morning as I was seeing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I appreciate that, Captain, and I just am trying to bore down a little bit on some of your approximations given the fact that you had other duties certainly starting about midday and that you stopped taking records of approximately 9.30, and we know from your notes that at approximately noon time you went down to a meeting with General Forand to the ARSK, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes. My notes are showing that at 12.10 to 1300 there was a meeting with General Forand and have I a recollection of that. But why there is no indication of the number of shell that landed, because there were, 0950 to 1210, I don't know why there is no entry in this little book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But suffice it to say, Captain, that your testimony on the approximate amount of shells reflects what you saw but also what you heard. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Please say the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you offered an assessment concerning the amount of shells that you say fell on Knin, that reflects an estimate of what you saw but also what you heard. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yeah, most -- most of what I saw, but also from what I heard, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you also note here that at 8.03, there was outgoing shell fire -- outgoing fire 300 metres out from the camp. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes, I can read 0803, outgoing 300 metre out from camp and three question mark, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that, sir, was outgoing fire by the ARSK, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I cannot say. I don't know. That's why there are question mark there. It was strange that there was outgoing fire 30 metre -- 300 metres out from the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Captain, it was outgoing fire from terrain that was controlled at that time by the ARSK, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I cannot even see where was that ground from my window. So I cannot say that it was ground that was controlled by the ARSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I mean as you sit here, Captain, do you think it was ground that was covered by the ARSK or do you think the HV was already in Knin 300 metres from the UN Sector South camp?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if you want to take a break now or you want me to keep going. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It looks as if this is a right time to have a break. Mr. Kehoe, could you give us any impression and could other Defence counsel give us any impression on how much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, probably just finish in the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I hear from other counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. I have about 30 minutes of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Same for me, Your Honour. Thank you. Perhaps less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That means that there is a fair expectation, but I'm also looking to you, Mr. Hedaraly, for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Not at the moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that means that there is a fair expectation that we could conclude the testimony of this witness today. We'll have a break and resume at a quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it is of any consolation to the parties, our late start is due to being very busy not on other matters but busy on this case during the break. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just during the break I was able to correct or find the error in that exhibit that I tendered at the beginning of today's session. In column 7 there was a transcription error and a decision by the state prosecutor's office. The word "conviction" was put in where word "indictment" should have been inserted. We're in the process of correcting that and uploading it into e-court, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll wait and see. Then one of the issues which is of some urgency, and Mr. Gilbert, I hope that you will forgive us for spend two or three minutes on another matter which is unrelated to your testimony. I would like to put on the record the Chamber's decision granting the Gotovina's request for a stay of the time-limit under Rule 73 (C) pending the issuance of the Chamber's reasons for admitting witness Zdravko Janic's statement under Rule 92 ter. On Friday, the 11th of July, 2008, the parties were informed of a decision taken by the Chamber with regard to an request filed by Gotovina Defence on the 10th of July. This concerned the request for a stay of the time limited for requesting certification under Rule 73 (C) of the Chamber's 8 of July 2008 decision on the Defence's objections to the admission of Zdravko Janic suspect interview under Rule 95. The Gotovina Defence requested that it be granted a stay pending the issuance of the Chamber's written reasons for its decision granting admission of witness Zdravko Janic's statement under Rule 92 ter, the reasons for this being that both decisions related to the admission into evidence of Zdravko Janic suspect interview. The Chamber would now like to put on the record that this request was grant and that the Gotovina Defence is informed that it will have seven days from the issuing of the reasons for admitting witness Zdravko Janic statements pursuant to Rule 92 ter in order to file any request for certification against both of the Chamber's decisions concerning this witness. That's now on the record. The Chamber could imagine that you become nervous, Mr. Misetic, if you would not have not known about this decision. Then, Mr. Kehoe, are you ready to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- continue. Then please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Captain, in paragraph 23 of your statement you noted that the estimates of the amount of shells coming into Knin by Colonel Leslie was high. Do you see that sir?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Seems a little bit high, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Colonel, did most of the people in the headquarters, UN Sector South headquarters defer to Leslie, given his rank and his professed artillery expertise?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No, nobody. It was just a personal comment of myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That was your personal view.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes, about the number and -- could you rephrase the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm talking about Leslie's high estimates. Did people in Sector South defer to Leslie because of his rank and because of his professed expertise in artillery?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I do, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You do?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now in paragraph 20 of your statement you note that you were -- the last sentence you say: "I remember because I was surprised that shells would be fired at night." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On the evening of the 4th were you aware of the military situation in the Knin area?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Not exactly sure of the military situation in the Knin area, but we did drive downtown that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, on the night of the 4th, let me read you something that Colonel Leslie said, and this is from a video D123. He says: "Taking Knin, no. We have no reports of Croatians being in direct fire range of Knin and there are still lots of Serbs in Knin and in the surrounding hills." D106, General Mrksic on behalf of the ARSK: "We are maintaining contact, our forces withdrew to positions for the direct defence of Knin. The other range of units are successfully holding their positions." Are you aware of continued fighting going on in Knin on the evening of the 4th, going into the morning of the 5th?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No. I think that the only thing that was going on in Knin that night, there were some small arm fire on a there were some -- a few, I estimated to 30, artillery shell landing in Knin, and there was not a big bad willing going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you aware of any troop movements through Knin?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No, I don't think there were any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, do you know that, sir, or is that your speculation?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: That's the best of my recollection that there was no -- there was no fighting or heavy fighting or movement in Knin. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me turn your attention to the actual shelling situation. And if I could bring up first P596. Prosecution 596. Is that -- is that P596, Mr. Usher -- Mr. Registrar? Now, sir, that is the photograph that was initially put into evidence, something that was taken on the fall, late November of last year. Let me show you a photograph -- two photographs and I want to show you it via Sanction than would be 1D38-0089, and I would like you to focus on the little shed as the reference point. The reference point on the left is the photograph that just came into evidence, P596. And the photograph on the right is from a video that was filmed on the morning of the 4th of August, 1995, by a UN employee inside headquarters. Now, Captain, is that what the area looked like or how you observed it back on the morning of the 4th of August, 1995? And I'm talking about the fog in the distance as well as the tree. That's over to the right-hand side of the photograph. Is that how it looked?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yeah, there is a tree there that has been cut, right? If it's the same little house, I would say that's the view that I had in the morning on the 5th, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So as you look over to the right-hand side, your view is obstructed by the tree, right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And likewise, because of the fog and smoke in the distance, your view is also -- was also obstructed on the 4th, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: But did you say was it on the 4th or the 5th?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is the 4th.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: The 4th, okay. Yes, there were some fog, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'd like to move this item into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes exhibit number D569.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D569 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Kehoe, there seems to be no issue as far as admissibility is concerned. The witness has answered questions about it. Nevertheless, these two pictures taken together are raising quite some puzzles for me. Angle of view, trees growing smaller over the years and of course you could -- apparently other structures, for example, if you would like at the right-hand side of the oval there seems to be something of a small structure as well which doesn't appear on the later one. It -- just for you to note.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Judge. If I can just put this in a reference point. The left-hand photograph of course is P596, the photograph that the OTP put in. The right hand is a still that we took from a video that was provided by the OTP. What we have attempted to do is, using that reference point, and we can give more frames to the Trial Chamber both left and right to maybe focus this little building in a little better. But this was something that has been purported to us in sending to us by the OTP as having been taken on the 4th of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But of course then questions arise such as was it taken from the third floor, was it taken from the bottom, what could you see over the tree, the trees which at least look far higher on the right picture than they look on the left one. So, therefore, I -- I fully accept that it is important to look at contemporaneous photographs or movies as well and not only to the situation as it appeared to be at a later stage but the comparison is -- seems to me to be rather complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is, Judge, and what we've tried to do is obviously our photograph or the juxtaposition of a photograph that was taken in late November of 1997 well into the fall, as my colleague has so properly pointed out, as opposed to something -- a timely photograph that took place the same day in the middle of the summer -- I'm sorry, it's 2007, not 1997, but the exact date I think gives the Trial Chamber as the witness pointed out an accurate view of, number one, the fact there was a tree obstructing his view on the right-hand side, and number two, quite importantly, what the horizon was like between fog and smoke. And, Your Honour, we will gladly take this OTP video and provide additional frames on both sides and maybe it could become yet clearer. We just believe that the juxtaposition of these two photographs at this point would be instructive not only for the Chamber but for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I did share with you what puzzles my mind, I think it's fair, and I don't think that by just the two or three questions we have resolved what puzzles my mind, and just for you to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.
