utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me talk to you about several angles, Captain, on that day and I would like to turn, first, 1D38-0084. Now, Captain, this is the photograph of P597, and the areas the two hills that you had previously talked about in your supplemental statement are A and B. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. And this is what you talked about when you observed shell fire on the hill. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: In my testimony, I mentioned behind a small hill and it's one of those two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. And, of course, when this -- when you were there at the time, it was August and this was significantly grown up with trees and leaves, et cetera, right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You don't recall?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's go to the next slide. This is a spatial view of the area from your location in UN Sector South with no elevation to it. If we can go to the next -- and we designate the two hills again, A and B. If we can go to the next slide. Now, you notice again we have A and B and your angle. And are you familiar, Captain, of -- I mean, do you know where these rounds landed when you saw them going in and about these hills?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Just tell me which of my statement you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you gave us a supplemental sheet from the Office of the Prosecutor concerning these two locations designating them as A and B and you just gave us an explanation during the course of your testimony about one of the small hills being hit. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: It was behind the small hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. So it was behind the small hill?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yeah. 0855, two round under fire heavy behind small hill. That's what I compare the small hill and I refer to it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know what is being targeted?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No. It just -- it just hit behind the small hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So if we go through either one of these targets, and you can pick either hill, the 1 being the Tvik factory, the 2 being the Elektroprivreda power distribution plant, 3 the Kinjacka factory, 4 the diesel depot, perhaps the railway maintenance yard, 5 the RSK state security. You have no idea what the HV was firing at, do you?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No. The only thing I can report is what I have seen and write in my notebook at that time. It was behind the small hill and I don't know what was hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Captain, are you familiar with these various --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said, well, you gave us a supplemental sheet from the Office of the Prosecutor concerning these two locations. Has the Chamber received any such thing? I mean, in order to follow the testimony, of course, we should be able to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I can just read it to you, Your Honour. I mean, it says that he also identified on P543, one of these exhibits, that the small hill he referred to in his contemporaneous notes of the shelling was one of the two hills in the picture. Hard copies of these pictures have also been placed in the Defence locker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because that is not evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I do understand that you indicated that one of these two hills, I think you said in earlier testimony, but the Chamber was unaware of the supplemental sheet, which it now appears to cover exactly the same as what you now testified in Court. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: As a matter of course we don't sent those to the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm not --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: -- if you want us to do that in the future or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm not complaining about it, but if someone makes reference to a certain document the Chamber is not aware of, then it's not more than logical, I would say, that the Chamber inquires into what the document is about and that's what I did and it turns out to be that it's giving exactly the same information as the witness gave during his testimony. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us go to the next slide. Now, this is the -- if we just orient you, Captain, this would be the -- basically the angle you were talking about as you're looking over hill B, would it not? And --

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: What you're say is that my observation point from the window --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: -- this yellow --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's your observation point.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yeah, let's say, well, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can we go to the next slide? So and with regard to these targets, sir, if these -- and I'm just saying if these individual items were targets, you would have seen a series of artillery fire throughout this area, wouldn't you? I'm not telling you to say that there are targets or not. I'm saying that if the shelling was taking place at all these areas we put in the map, you would have seen an array of fire going from behind hill B all the way over to the left-hand side of this photograph, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just for a frame of reference, sir, each of these targets --

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: A and B, that's what you're talking about, A and B?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the targets that we have, 1 through 5, are the geometry as put forth on the angle 1 through 5 so you see that juxtaposed behind those hills.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yeah, I can -- okay, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So if you saw an array of shell fire from this area, as you say in your statement that the shells fell all over town, assuming these were targets, you would have seen shelling all the way over from your mound point B to the left-hand side of this photo, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the question. But maybe I can state what I saw from the window. I saw that hill indicated as B, I saw that hill as indicated as A, and I saw some artillery shell falling behind those hill, and I saw specifically at 0855, as I note in my book, two round behind small hill. I don't know which one of those two it is. I saw that, and I saw a lot more to the left of hill A.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Which was the town of Knin. So that's what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We will get to that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me, I'm sorry, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I know the Court has some concerns about more than one lawyer rising but I raise what I hope is a general matter in connection -- that I have raised before in connection with demonstrative evidence like this. To the extent it is helpful, of course the Prosecution welcomes such photographs and aids, but in this particular case, I'm try to go sort it out as well, we're seeing it for the first time today, and the yellow dotted line appears to be significant but it appears to me that could be drawn at any number of angles from that particular balcony going out in any number of direction and depict something different. I thought I also understood, by the way, that the witness was talking about the other balcony in connection with his observations, but if the -- if the relative precision versus the relative generality of the assistance that can be offered by the document is made clear, I think we'll be better -- the Court will be better assisted and so will the parties. But if it's a matter of fine precision, then it's also a matter of knowing precisely where it was taken from, precisely what the angle of view was and a lot more variables need to be fleshed out and the Prosecution needs to be aware of it in order to understand the utility or limitations of the document. So this is a general matter, so I'm sorry to intervene, but it's something that's concerned me --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I respond to that? I mean this is their photograph. This is the photograph that they dropped in our locker last night. The line in the middle is the location of the photographer, based on the evidence given to us by the Prosecutor, we then did these calculations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, which balcony is the -- I think as a matter of fact that I ask some additional questions especially out of concern whether we have the right picture in front of us. Mr. Tieger, if this Chamber really feels that it is not assisted by this kind of reconstructions, I think you know the Chamber well enough to know that the Chamber will not hide this. That's one. Second, of course, we should not forget that the further the distance, the less the impact of five or ten metres difference from a point of view. I mean if you're standing 100 metres before a hill, a small hill, then it makes quite a difference -- it can at least make quite a difference whether you move to the left or to the right a couple of metres. The further the distance, the less impact it has. So, therefore, I do appreciate that your concerns that the Chamber would not be assisted. And as you said also the parties are not assisted, then I take it the OTP is not assisted by it. Of course it seems that Mr. Kehoe thinks that it assists him in getting a better view on what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While that's understood, Mr. Kehoe, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I just accept what the Prosecution gives us and work with the elements that they gave us. They provided us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, let's -- Mr. Tieger has expressed his concern whether this would assist or at least assist the Chamber. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour, at this time I'll offer into evidence 1D38-0084, this array of photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think as an additional matter, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: -- THE foundation, because the witness did not recognise any of these alleged targets and then what these line of sight, so once again I think it may be something -- I don't know who prepared it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Targets are already in evidence in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's keep -- let's keep matters simple. Mr. Gilbert, what is put to you by Mr. Kehoe is the following: That if the only thing you saw is that the shells were falling behind these hills, then Mr. Kehoe, on the basis of the evidence presented to this Chamber, takes the position that there's quite a range in the -- from left to right behind these hills, where in the view of the Defence and on the basis of what the Defence has presented as evidence to this Chamber, that there are a lot of targets that could be hit or targeted behind these hills. The question is, I think, which Mr. Kehoe did put to you, were you aware of those possible targets and do you have any additional information which would lead you to reasonably assume that the shells falling behind these hills were not falling upon the targets Mr. Kehoe earlier showed to you. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I was not aware of any target. There were shell falling behind those hill. There were shell falling out to the left of those hill. There were shell during that one -- 4th and 5th of August until noon. There were shell falling all over the place. I had and I still never -- I don't think that it was intended for a specific target. I think it was harassing fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And could you tell us what's the basis for this thought, apart from because what Mr. Kehoe puts to you, is that in the full width of what you describe, that is the two hills, that behind the hills, for the Defence, there are potential targets. So if that full range, Mr. Kehoe wonders how you could determine that this is harassing fire rather than targeting any of these military objectives.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the general context there was firing all over Knin. You know, were specifically talking to 0855, when in my notes I put behind the small hill. So somebody is asking me could you identify the small hill. I'm saying it's one of those two. Was it a military -- was there a military target behind it, maybe yes; maybe not. I don't know. But at the time and still now, I'm not thinking that it was hitting a military target. Because from the morning of the 4th until noon on the 5th, there was artillery fire, under my estimated amount of shell, all over Knin. So I don't -- I still don't think that it was intended to a specific military target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think we have explored sufficiently what objective data there are and what the -- apparently what the thoughts of the witness are. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we offer 1D38-0084 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether welcome or not, is it admissible or not, Mr. Hedaraly?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We have no objection to the admissibility, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Hedaraly. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes exhibit number D570.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D570 is admitted into evidence and that is the whole series.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just that whole series.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There is more as the angle moves so we will go to 1D38-0083 because the witness said that he observed shelling to the left of this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that is what comes next.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The series as we have seen them until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you noted for us that you stated that there was artillery fire to the left of the photograph that we previously referenced and I asked you, looking at the -- shifting over on to the other side of what you designated as mound A, you see one, the Senjak barracks; two, the Agroprevreda depot; and three, the Tvik factory. Are you aware of those locations?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No. That is the first time I read those names there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But there was artillery fire straight away left of the mound that you had designated as A, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: There was artillery fire all over town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we'll offer 1D38-0083 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Once again, Your Honour, he has not identified those specific issues but I guess if this is not an admissibility issue, then we won't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes exhibit number D571.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D571 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me bring up -- thank you, Mr. President. Let me bring up 1D38-0001 and this is it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While that is done, Mr. Kehoe, I find in the previously just admitted, that just admitted I see a number 76 which I don't know what it is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can we flip back to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you have access to it -- to another copy, then I'm not going to -- 76, it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't see the 76 on that photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just close to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Oh, that is a grid reference, Judge. When you take these Google Earth maps, the grid references on the Google Earth --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. It's a grid reference. Just for me to know. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can I go to two up. Go in reverse order, page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, this is yet a further angle to the left, Captain, from the UN Sector South headquarters looking downtown. Do you recognise this sir?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And let me go to the next slide, page 2. Now, sir, if I can just blow that up a bit, I have listed here 17 locations that have been previously admitted into evidence. And for reference the all these items were set forth in D131. Are you familiar with all of these locations, sir, and just take a look at the chart to the left.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: ARSK barracks must be number 10. I recognise that. And I don't see the white parliament building. I don't know if it is named somewhere in there but I cannot figure out on that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is number 3, sir, at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Number 3, parliament, okay. And the hospital, I don't know if you're calling it an old hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Is there just one?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You're talking about the hospital that was in use?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Way over to the right, the white building way over to the right.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Is it circled there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: That is it not a place that I would recognise. Okay. All the other one, I do not recognise, I do not recognise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, can we go to the first slide. Sir, we've taken these 17 items in these locations with the two mounds, the hill to the left and the hill to the right, as reference points. Sir, if all of these locations were shelled at some point during the day on the 4th or the 5th, it would have looked to you like the shelling, as you say in paragraph 9 of your statement, the shells fell all over town.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I guess we would need I mean the actual calculations or the basis. There is no way for to us test the accuracy of sort of if that accurately represents those locations that were described in the previous slide and that is actually the -- and questions being put to the witness. It just --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, I think that -- I mean the logic behind this is clear. The data on the map are clear as well. The earlier evidence is clear also. Therefore, I would allow Mr. Kehoe to continue. At the same time, Mr. Kehoe, the issue of potential targeting what you identified as military targets is not a new issue with which you could surprise the Prosecution. Therefore, with this technical elaboration of those issues, I think it would be good if you would give notice to the Prosecution in advance on how you put this into material which will be put to a witness, because, otherwise, it might be almost impossible to verify the accuracy of it, and at the same time, of course, that might cause that we would have to re-call a witness. I mean, if it is something new, then of course I can imagine that you would say I'd rather not disclose this already to the Prosecution, but if it comes to these technical details, then where the issue is clearly there, I mean, if you read the statement of the witness, it of course came immediately to my mind, but whatever the merits of it are, therefore under those circumstances I think it might a good idea to share some of the technical elaboration that the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will gladly take them through it. Frankly, it's simple geometry, but I think and I appreciate that it -- it may look a tad bit more complex than it is, but that is what it is. It's just simple geometry taking the targets that they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't have to -- you don't have to explain to me, Mr. Kehoe, that it is simple geometry apart from, of course, at this moment in these pictures that the depth doesn't appear anymore which of course is clear from the picture itself, so I'm not surprised by that. But even in geometry, sometimes mistakes are made and what Mr. Hedaraly is asking is give us an opportunity to verify the accuracy of your work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You know, and absolutely, Judge, and if I'm mistaken on the geometry I will stand corrected. We have tried to check this geometry over and over but please I would like the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, there's no blame at this point.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT REPORTER
utterances.text: One at a time, please, one at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The issue simply is whether if we are coming to this technical presentation of the geometry, whether for the purpose of giving an opportunity to the Prosecution to verify whether they agree with you that it was accurately done, whether there would be a possibility to give them in advance access to this very technical material.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. If I do these geometric calculations again, I will gladly do that. I trust there won't be many more of these. Nevertheless I'm certainly gladly to share the calculations and how it was done with my friends across the bar and see how -- and let them check how we did it and our conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that was what Mr. Hedaraly was asking for. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know how you want to do this. I was offered 1D38-0001 into evidence at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objections Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes exhibit number D572.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D572 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Captain, would it be accurate to say that as you were standing on the balcony, you had no idea of what potential targets there were other than the RSK barracks that you notified -- that you talked about before? Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: What is accurate is I was not watching from the balcony. I was watching from my office window, which is neither of those angle of view. And what is accurate is that the shelling was all over Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And my follow-up question to that is you as you sit here have no idea what the target was of that shelling, do you, or the targets were of that shell, do you? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In fact, sir, when -- you in fact in your statement or in your note when you say that the target of the bombardment was the civilians and this is in your article on page 593, page 3, you also say on 591, your notes at 543 --

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I do not follow you now. The article?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just go to 543 -- go to 591.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: My article?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: First your article.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: What page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I insist on short breaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I made similar mistakes recently, and that made me even more aware how important it is to give an opportunity to the transcriber and the interpreters to reflect what is said accurately on the record. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In page 3 of your article, you note that the targets of the bombardment were the civilians.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I recall that, but I would like to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Page 3, last paragraph in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It is page 4 of the French, if that assists the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm reading in English. I will read it in French because it was writed in French. Where is it? It's page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Page 3 in the English, sir, and maybe counsel can help with the French.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Page four of the French. It is the fifth line, fifth or sixth line, "they are the target of" ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The exodus of majority of civilians had started. They are the target of this shelling."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you said that, sir, because you were unaware of any other potential targets. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I said that because I thought that at the moment and I wrote it in an article to public which is -- you know the intent of the article was for public reading, not to come in court, and that's why the reason why I put it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Take a look at 591, your notes. P591. And the time entry of 5.43.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: It is on the second day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: First day, 5.43.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: But I started timing at 5.43. Hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you read the entry for 5.43?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: "Notice no fire by location of ARSK seems a bit heavily."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you wrote that article knowing, Captain, that you had written in your notes that the ARSK headquarters had been hit heavily at 0543 on the morning of the 4th, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I think that mischaracterises. There is no mention of headquarters in the notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You hit the ARSK on the morning of the 4th?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: What I meant by that was the barracks that we talked earlier. At 0543 the shell were landing close to that barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So I reiterate, you wrote that in your article knowing full well that you had documented that an ARSK facility had been hit on 0543 on the 4th of August, right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No right, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can just have one second here, Your Honour. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let us turn your attention to the morning of the 4th and your activities, and you did in fact go to the ARSK headquarters with General Forand at approximately midday on the 4th, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it was the ARSK headquarter. But we went to a place where there was an ARSK representative, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And prior to that time, had there been communication with the RSK authorities?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Not myself. It was the headquarter Sector South contact, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me play you a video, D327, if I may. This is two ARSK officials on the morning of the 4th, talking about communications with the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Go back to the beginning, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] At 4.14 I received a phone call from liaison officer from headquarters who was our government liaison officer for UNPROFOR that he had received information from an operational organ within UNPROFOR from Sector South command that the Croats would say be attacking us. Miroslav Sekolic: We were informed 18 times by various officers, French, these informing us we will be attacked in the morning at 5.00 a.m."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On channel 5 I did not receive French translation, but I don't know where the problem lies, and for the completeness of the record --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Could we replay it, Judge? It's very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we please replay the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] at 4.15 I received a phone call from a liaison officer from headquarters who was our government's liaison officer of UNPROFOR that he had received information from an operational organ within UNPROFOR from Sector South command that the Croats would be attacking us. Miroslav Sekolic: "We were informed 18 times by various officers, French, these and others, informing us that we would be attacked in the morning at 5.00 a.m."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Captain, were you the French officer who called the RSK headquarters to tell them that they were going to be attacked?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No, I was not, I'm sure not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And do you know who was?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How much French officers worked at UN Sector South on the morning of the 4th, French-speaking officers beside you, General Forand, and Major Bellerose?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Major Dussault. But what I think that may refer to is another -- when I heard it I thought it was from French forces officer liaison officer, or from Knin, but it was certainly not me, and a rough thing, maybe four or five people speaking French from the UN headquarters Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge that this phone call going to the RSK to tell them that the attack was coming?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you went with, your notes P591 reflects, and this is at the third page, reflects a meeting at approximately midday. Do you see that, sir.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: 12.10 to 13, meeting with Karpalak and press conference in Knin, yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before we go get to that, you mentioned some Canadian officers that were French-speaking. Were there any officers from France at UN Sector South in Knin?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Maybe a couple. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You don't recall?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No. I would have to look into our nominal roll.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in the morning of this meeting in midday, and I turn your attention to P543. And as we're coming up with that exhibit, who went to UN Sector South at midday with you?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: We went to some kind of ARSK barracks where there were people there. That's what you mean, it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I apologise. Who went to the meeting with the RSK at midday on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Me, the driver, General Forand, for sure. Probably a UNHCR rep, a UN civilian rep, and maybe another person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Roberts go?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Maybe, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did Colonel Ratsouk go?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I don't remember that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel Nikolai Ratsouk?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I don't know that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, what was the purpose of the meeting that you went to?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: It says there meeting with Karpalak and press conference in Knin. I recall being in that room. That was a crowded room, I was inside with the people when that took place. There was maybe six or seven people from RSK and five, six, from the UN representative. That was a crowded room. I don't know what was the meeting of that and I see there that it says and press conference in Knin. I don't know that there was a press conference. I don't know if it was a joint, I don't know. I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This is -- I was looking for P343, I apologise. Now during this meeting, the UN provided the RSK with a radio, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I don't know what are you referring to. Just give me the name of the paper, because with the number I cannot refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm going to bring up a exhibit here on the screen, P343.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: That's what I see there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. If we -- on the left --

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: [Inaudible].

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is a sitrep of 4 August 1995 and if we can go into what is been designated as page 5. It's a -- keep going, please. If I may, it's page 5 at the top. Three more pages in, please. One more. Well, we can just move ahead and ask the question. Captain, did the UN -- here it is. If we go to that paragraph towards the end of the meeting with the warring factions, it talk about the meeting with Colonel Kosta Novakovic at approximately 11.30. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Just give me paragraph, H, I?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Paragraph H.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: H?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just take a look at paragraph H.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: One, two, three, four, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's what we had. Can you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes, I'm reading it through the second paragraph now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Okay. I have read paragraph H.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if you read that -- that last sentence in the third paragraph down in H, it notes: "[Indiscernible] commander RSK stated he speak on the radio and tell the people to allow the UN to help. It was agreed that HQ Sector South would remain in contact with HQ ARSK." Now to do that, did the UN -- do you see that, sir, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I will read it again. "Commander RSK state that he speak on the radio ... " Okay. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, to do that did the UN provide the ARSK with a UN radio.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No. I'm reading that now for the first time and what I understand is that he would speak on his own radio channel and tell his ARSK personnel to allow UN to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I am talking to them about that -- the and I will tell you that you General Forand in P330, paragraph -- page 5, paragraph 4, said that, "we provided them for the purposes of the coordinating humanitarian assistance a radio." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did the UN provide the RSK authorities for -- did they provide them with an APC?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't know, and I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you recall one way or the other, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No, no, I don't recall anything. But I don't think we did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, the evacuation in fact began to be planned at that meeting, did it not?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No. I would say no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me read you P401, if we could bring that up. This is a presentation by General Forand and if I could have -- if we just use the numbers the 0530638. And if we can go to the last paragraph on that page, General Forand says: "I understand now that the RSK supreme defence took the decision at about noon on 4 August to abandon the Krajina." Did you know that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I would not be as precise as General Forand did on his notes or speak -- briefing there, but that -- yeah, around the 4th or the 5th. But at some point, yeah, they did -- they took the decision to abandon, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, this says that the decision was made at noon on the 4th. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is a that -- accurate or based on your recollection?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: What I just told you what was my recollection, it was somewhere on the 4th or on the 5th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you went to a meeting -- I'll try to slow down here. You went to a meeting later on on the 4th and if we can go on and bring up P592.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, for the understanding of this document, the line "I understand now," is of course something that might be relevant. So if you put to the witness what happened or at least what was in this document I'd prefer to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General Forand said that he was at this meeting and then it became clear to from a variety of other information that they had planned the evacuation as of noon on the 4th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, this is the minutes of your -- or these are your notes, are they not, sir, of your evacuation -- I mean, excuse me, of the meeting that you went to at approximately 1800 on the 4th, as we can see from the first line?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in the first paragraph, there was an ARSK chief of residents evacuation. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know who that person was?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So based on your understanding at the time, there was an ARSK officer or an official that was specifically in charge of the residents of evacuation. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I would prefer to say that we were provided with that information at the meeting. I took note, and I wrote that as it was given to me. But it -- it looks like there was one person there that hold that title.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, at this meeting, sir, they had outlined -- and let me turn your attention to D182. D182. This is another memo of that meeting by Colonel Ratsouk. The date here says 8th of July, but the parties have stipulated that this is in fact an inaccurate date and it emanates from the meeting on the 4th of August. Now, in the centre of that paragraph it notes that the -- if you can just read that at the second paragraph in?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I will read the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Can I please be told who is Colonel Ratsouk.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel Ratsouk is one of the individuals that I've asked you whether or not he was at the meeting at noon time on the 4th.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I don't know him, but maybe it would help me to know who that person is. Is that a UN Sector South representative or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He is, sir.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: And can I know more about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He was Russian Sector South representative.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: And he was working with us at UN Sector South?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He was.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I have no recollection of that. I should have got my list. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He was UNCRO from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Attached to us. Attached to us, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Or to UNCRO, sir.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Okay. So he was with us, so I'll take that as -- I'm not sure, but I will take that. Okay. I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now. Let me show you one last document in conjunction with Mr. Ratsouk's comment and that would be D337, which is a cable from Mr. Akashi to Mr. Annan on the 4th of August. And we go to the -- after you look at the front page can we go to the last paragraph on the next page, paragraph 4. And blow up paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: So it's Akashi in Zagreb talking to New York?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: At what time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There's no stamp on. There's a stamp on it, sir, but there has been some question what the exact time is, but it is the 4th.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: It would be after 1900 at night. I don't know. Okay. I read it. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, so, at the time this meeting was ended, were you -- did you know that in fact the evacuation to Banja Luka had been planned and was going to take place or was taking place?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: The -- not by the UN, but the ARSK or the Serb authority in Knin, they were trying most probably to evacuate their people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And your understanding was that the evacuation was going to be to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No, I don't know where the evacuation was to go, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, did -- do you have any idea where Mr. Ratsouk -- Colonel Ratsouk or Mr. Akashi got the information that it was supposed to go to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now there was also some -- some reservation about providing fuel to the RSK in order for them to evacuate, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: My understanding that there was an intention from the UN to provide fuel not to the ARSK but to the civilian population in need.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, the paragraph 4 says that that had to be spoken about, there is a wide range of policy, political and military and logistical implications that must be examined with UNHCR before we can contemplate such a commitment and accordingly, Sector South has been advised by UNCRO to make no commitment to the Knin authorities other than the matter will be examined tomorrow. But fuel was given, anyway. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: What I saw is in front of our UN compound that there is older people that came with some tractor and some bicycle and motor bicycle and they were requesting fuel and that was given to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me shift subjects and cover a couple things that you mentioned in your statement and that had to do with after you became the refugee officer, as you say in paragraph 34 of your statement. And you note in paragraph 34 that -- excuse me, paragraph 35 that "people were too afraid to go back home. What I mean by afraid is afraid for their physical safety, they were worried about what would happen to them if they went back and no one could guarantee their safety. This is why most of the people ultimately went back to Serbia." Captain, let me ask you a question. When you were talking to refugees were in there, how many people told you they still had either husbands or sons that were still in the ARSK?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I had -- I never discussed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you never ask that question?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, turning to that issue, as you're in -- the refugee officer, how many soldiers actually were allowed into the base by the UN?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I think, to my recollection, one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yeah. And when we find out, he was sent out. And that was not an agreement. He came to the camp without proper identification or I don't know what, but when it was found out that he was in the camp, he was sent out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now you were, as you described, the refugee officer, and let me show you something -- read something to you from D514 from Major Bellerose. He notes on the second page of this article, "because we opened up the camp to displaced persons to provide security, there were few Serb soldiers that came to try to get refuge within our camp. So we said to them 'if you want to come in, you have to disarm, because if we let you in with weapons, we're putting ourselves at risk.'" Now, do you know anything about these soldiers that were allowed in that Major Bellerose is referring?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I would like to have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sure. If we can bring that up on the screen it is D514. It comes from an article called One Soldier's Story, Major Claude Bellerose. D154.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course we could look at it. But are you aware of soldiers required to disarm and then let into the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I became the refugee officer, the date is the 25th of August. So refugee has started from the 4th to the 25th. In that period, you know, I was just like another staff officer at the UN headquarters handling refugee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But whatever time, are you aware of soldiers given access to the camp but were required to disarm first?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. But there was one during my term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think you explained that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether there is any need then to give the details of Mr. Bellerose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's fine, Judge, I was just bringing it up because the witness wanted it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I just have a few more questions on this, Judge, and I will conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Captain, in addition to what captain -- Major Bellerose is talking about, were you aware of soldiers being taken from the Knin hospital and being brought into UN Sector South?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware, and it would not be adequate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What do you mean by adequate?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: It's not something that was in the policy to my knowledge to bring soldier on to our camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, there were 38 people who were turned over to the Croatian authorities because they were suspected of war crimes by the Croatian government, 38 individuals that were turned over by UN Sector South to Croatian authorities. And you were in charge -- you were the refugee officer at the time. Who were these 38 people?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I don't want to question the Defence but at what date?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: They were turned over in September of 1995, after you had become the refugee officer at the UN camp.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: To my recollection, we have not returned any people to the Croat authority while I was the refugee officer. I think I state somewhere when I went on leave, and that might be that time. Can we check that? If you give me the exact date --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It's paragraph 35.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. If you have the exact date of that, I would be willing to check, because must have been after the 16. Before the 16th those people were not turned in, if they were turned in after.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you were aware that the Republic of Croatia wanted the suspected war criminals, people suspected of war crimes that were in the custody of UN Sector South, you were aware of that, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, yeah they were looking for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just -- Mr. Hedaraly, were you referring to paragraph 34 or 35?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: 35 about when the witness was on leave which he was looking for to assess to be able to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I thought you were referring to the refugees that were wanted to be interviewed as --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I was referring to the date that he asked for when he was on leave. But you're right, that is also in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You were aware of that, weren't you, that these negotiations for the turning over of people suspected of war crimes was ongoing?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: What I was aware of is that the Croat wanted to have people in the camp that were suspected of war crime from their perspective, not from an UN perspective, you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And these negotiations with the Republic of Croatia were going on for six weeks after Operation Storm, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No. I would say one week after I was the refugee officer, approximately, so it gives me a specific date, some -- sometime around the 1st of September --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: 25 of August, paragraph 35.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yeah. But I mean one week after I became the refugee officer that those requests came in, you know, that they were looking for those name and all that. Just to situate it, it would be around the 1st of August that my recollection is they were looking for this list of war crime -- war crime -- just as we said earlier, you know, the -- they wanted a certain number of people because they allegedly, from their perspective, says that they wanted for a crime against what, and that was about the 1st of September, if I recall that's what we are looking for, the period, so I would say 1st September.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, you went on -- and then you went on leave, according to paragraph 35, from the 16th of September to the 7th of October. Did you come back to UN Sector South at that point?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you come back as the refugee officer?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No. There was no more refugee when I came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you came back did you ask how the request by the Republic of Croatia for the release of these suspected war criminals, how that was resolved?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No, did I not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You didn't ask one question?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you have no knowledge about the circumstances under which 38 individuals were turned over to the Republic of Croatia by UN Sector South?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. We will have a break until five minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Just for timing purposes, Mr. Kehoe has robbed me a lot of my thunder, and so I think I will only be about ten minutes, essentially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Gilbert, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Cayley, who is counsel for Mr. Cermak. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could have Defence Exhibit 226.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Captain Gilbert, if you could please direct your mind to August after the Croatian authorities had retaken Knin, my question for you in looking in this photograph, do you recall ever visiting these buildings?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Not 100 percent sure but this left building might be the one that we went to for the 4th of August, 1210 meeting that we discussed earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that would have been a meeting with the ARSK authorities?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes. What I was referring to, the small room when there were 12 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And after the ARSK authorities had left Knin and the Croatian authorities were back in charge in Knin, do you ever recall visiting that building again?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I have got to put this to you because I have instructions on this. So this is actually the building in which Mr. Cermak and his small team operated. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So when you say in your statement that when you met with Mr. Cermak on the 10th of August with General Forand, and I can direct you to that. It's paragraph 26 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You say that you met with Mr. Cermak in the white parliament building on or about -- around the 10th of August, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is it possible that you're mistaken about that, that you didn't in fact meet in the white parliament building?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: My initial impression was that it was in the white parliament building. Now that you're showing me that, it could have been that one. I don't recall 100 percent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. You said earlier in an answer to Mr. Kehoe that -- and this is actually toward the end of your cross-examination by him and you were speaking about the refugees in the camp and he was asking you about the Croatian authorities' desire to investigate them for war crimes. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Are you aware that the issue of screening the men in the camp for war crimes was something that was being discussed at a high level in Zagreb between the United Nations and the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes, most probably. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you were aware of that because you were close to General Forand.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Not really. It's because I was the refugee officer and they were asking a lot of question about what would happen to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: And I could not provide them any answer and that was a long process, and I tried to -- to reassure them, but by that I mean that it was a higher decision to return the refugee, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And in terms of this higher discussion process, were you aware that Mr. Akashi himself was involved in those discussions with representatives of the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, please, the witness could be shown D29.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, do you recall that in your response to Mr. Kehoe you stated: "What I was aware is that the Croats want to the have people in the camp that suspected of crimes from their perspective, not from UN perspective." Do you recall stating that?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yeah, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, please, we could look at the second page of the document, paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And, if, please, Captain Gilbert, you could look at the first two sentences in paragraph 5. And let me know when you've read them.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes, I have read them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, this is a document -- if you could go to the front page. Did you see this is a document from Mr. Akashi in Zagreb to Kofi Annan in New York?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yeah, I saw that, but is it the same one that was shown to me earlier and I went to the last paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, this is the same document.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Okay. So I saw that it was Akashi and I saw that it was those first two sentence, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So were you aware in August of 1995 that it was Mr. Akashi's view that the government of Croatia had a legitimate interest in actually seeking to determine if any of the men in the camp you were involved in war crimes? Were you aware that that was the UN view at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Not on the 7th of August. This document is dated 7th of August?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: So, at that time no. But when I was the refugee officer, it became known to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That --

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: They were looking for suspected war crime criminal.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But specifically my question is this: Were you aware at any time that Annan -- that -- I'm sorry, that Mr. Akashi had said that the Croatian authorities had a legitimate interest in seeking out those persons in the camp who they suspected of war crimes?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No. But is this paragraph 4 exactly what it states? I --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you can go back to it, let's go and you can have another look at it. That's what he says.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: At which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's paragraph 5, it's the second sentence.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: I was not aware of that time but I'm reading those three or four first line and Mr. Akashi saying has a legitimate interest, so that's his -- that's what he wrote, so he must have meant that. But at that time I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And he was the special representative of the Secretary-General wasn't he, in Croatia, at this time?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So he -- in essence, his view was the view of the UN in Croatia, yes?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cayley. Mr. Kuzmanovic, are you ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gilbert, Mr. Kuzmanovic will now cross-examine you. He is counsel for Mr. Markac. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your statement, P589, if that could be put up on the screen, please. The first paragraph of your statement and if you have that in front of you in the binder, feel free to refer to it. Sir, do you have the statement in the binder in front of you? It might be easier for you to refer to it in your binder than looking at it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: But I don't know what is P584.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It's your witness statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor in January of 2008.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Okay. I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. The first paragraph says you became a captain in 1987. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Of course it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. I was just unsure, because if you look at P593, and that will probably have to be pulled up on the screen for you, on the first page. The beginning part of it says: "After spending two years as a regimental Sergeant Major I have since 8 July 1995 been performing the duties of military assistant to the commander of Sector South." Can you explain that, please?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain in your article here by Captain Alain Gilbert, P593, you describe yourself as a regimental Sergeant Major. Can you explain the difference between your rank and what a regimental Sergeant Major is?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: This there is a mistake in the translation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: What I -- if it has been translated okay, it would have said a regimental adjutant. That is what it says in French.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So --

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So the English translation is incorrect. You have been a captain since 1987?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Why don't we stick with P593 for a moment. Did you have a chance to compare this translation to your original, by the way?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes. Last night I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Other than that mistake, are there any other mistakes that you happened to catch?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. The second paragraph talks about how the headquarters is made up and that I'm assuming is the headquarters of Sector South. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The -- it discusses the make-up of general officers from the various nations, and the second sentence says, and I will read it to you and then I'll have a question for you: "Some of them are lazy and rarely see the need to work to the end of the week. Others have the habit of turning towards Mecca at certain times of the day." And then you end it: "Be that as it may, I assure you once more of my pride in belonging to the category of Canadian." Now, my question to you is, did you feel that you and your Canadian comrades had some better level of professionalism and experience than the other members of the Sector South staff?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And was there a problem that you had with other people praying and using their religion during their work?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the need for the comment of habit of turning towards Mecca at certain times of the day?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Because that is what was taking place in the headquarter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like you to go to the next page, please. The second paragraph talks about many people reading this will have served in UN headquarters. Well, who was your target audience for this article?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: The member who have -- [Interpretation] The members who subscribed to Citadelle, la Citadelle. It's a magazine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So it is a Canadian audience, in other words?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, Canadian and more regimental audience.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. And feel free -- I know French is your native tongue. Feel free if there is some problem to refer to that. We have excellent interpreters, so -- The remainder of that paragraph discusses, among other things, that there are -- and I will read that section: "I would confirm that the problem of command coordination and control is repeated in the absence of political solutions which I admit are difficult to adopt. Each organism gets bogged down in justifying its existence, its role in the field and the chain of command which directs it, whether it is the UN civilian police, the UNHCR, or the civilian representatives. The military commander is thus confronted by a multitude of political obstacles which he could well do without. This is what I observe there." And my question to you is: This difficulty in coordination and in problems of command and control, is that something that you observed in Knin during your time there, in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes, yes, this is what the article is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that in essence often times, for lack of a better term, the right hand in Sector South didn't know what the left hand was doing because of this lack of control?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: If you could be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure. You said that there was a difficulty in command and coordination among the various organisations that were headquartered in Sector South over which General Forand had command. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: He was the Sector South commander. Not sure if the highest UN or civilian representative there was really under him. They were at some kind of level, but he was certainly the military authority commander, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So there was difficulty in communications within Sector South despite who was in military command. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And that was in a time when there was absolutely no fighting going on. Correct? I mean you got there in June of 1995, right, so before Operation Storm there was some difficulty even before there was any kind of fighting going on in knowing essentially what was going on and who was speaking with whom.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes, in a lesser extent, but, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: When you served in Sarajevo in July of 1992, were you serving under General McKenzie?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: He was the Sarajevo UN commander there, so there's all kind of unit working for him. I was part of the unit that was serving for him. But not directly. You know, I have never met him, but I served under him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'd like to go back to your statement, please. And before we do that, I guess, you served as an aide to General Forand, you stated. What exactly did you do? Can you give us a description of your role before Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Agenda, overseeing the resident staff. I also saw myself as somehow his body-guard or being personally responsible for his security and accompanied him during various Sector South unit visits before Operation Storm, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe what you mean by agenda? Would you set the agenda for the day?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. Not for the day itself, but for planning of visit or conference in Zagreb or something. I was making the liaison with the authority and putting the calendar together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Who else was on that resident staff?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: There was Corporal Desroches, who was living there. He was a driver. And master corporal Ellis, the cook.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Anyone else?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any interpreters?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Was your position in terms of the things that you did the same other than you mentioned you were refugee -- in charge of the refugees. Did your position change at all after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yeah, it changed when I became the refugee officer, but I would say between the period of the 5th of August until the became the refugee officer, we were to create new accommodation on Sector South, new -- because we were living outside so I was responsible to put that up, and less of the calendar, and, let's say the day-to-day running of the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you the person -- would you be -- let me try to think of a different way to phrase this. When General Forand would go to a meeting, would you be with him at all the meetings?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes. But not all of them. There's some in my statement that I was not there and I know that General Forand went to other meeting without me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, at that time Colonel Leslie was the Chief of Staff. What was your relationship with Colonel Leslie?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: He was the Chief of Staff until, I would say, around the 4th of August and the new Chief of Staff came in, and because of the war it could not left, so he was still in the headquarter for four or five days, I would estimate, and I had a good relationship with Colonel Leslie also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like you to refer to paragraph 35 of your statement, please.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And you -- in this paragraph you discussion the refugees. And I'll go to the sentence that starts with "they" on the third line, "they," and I'm presuming that those are the Serb refugees. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: "Were worried about what would happen to them if they went back and no one could guarantee their safety. This is why most of the people ultimately went back to Serbia." And my question to you is, is it your understanding that these refugees originally came from Serbia into Sector South and then went back to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No. My understanding is that they were from Serb ethnic origin living in Knin, I would say, for at least the last three years, and then there was no other -- no other choice than going back to Serbia, Belgrade or going back to -- I'm mentioning Serbia but I think that when they left the camp they all went back to Belgrade and were left there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware at any time of any efforts that were undertaken by the Croatian government to try to ensure their safety if they stayed?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Oh, yes, that was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So you, as refugee officer, were aware of statements made by the Croatian government to try to keep these people from leaving. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes. When General Cermak came and met with the refugee, that was the message that was passed to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to refer to paragraph 29, please. And the third line, which is -- starts: "When we got there," meaning to General Forand's residence. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: "We could see that the entire house had been thrashed, completely vandalized allegedly by the Croatian soldiers, special police, military police and the Croat occupation forces in general." Now, is there anyone else that you wanted to add to that list?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that -- can you identify what a special police member looks like?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you identify what a military police member looks like?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What do they look like?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: They had a special brassar [phoen] identifying them as military police Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see this alleged vandalisation occur?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN GILBERT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
